title: Separated at Birth
blurb: Two capabilities that sound identical until one fact flips — learn to hear the difference the exam listens for.

pairs.dimension: identifying what is mentioned vs scoring the opinion about it

a.text: From support tickets, list every product name, person, and date mentioned.
a.why: Entities identify who/what is mentioned — people, dates, organizations (histack: 'categorizes specific things').

b.text: From the same tickets, determine whether customers feel positive, negative, or neutral.
b.why: Opinion polarity is sentiment — the exam's #1 confused pair (17 co-occurrences).

pairs.dimension: which direction the audio conversion runs

a.text: Transcribe a call-center recording so agents can search the conversation.
a.why: Audio in, text out — recognition. 'Transcribe' is the giveaway verb.

b.text: A navigation app reads turn-by-turn directions aloud with the en-US-Ava neural voice.
b.why: Text in, audio out — synthesis. SSML and voice names like en-US-Ava:DragonHDLatestNeural belong to synthesis only.

pairs.dimension: crossing languages vs staying in the same language

a.text: A conference app listens to a French speaker and produces live English captions for the audience.
a.why: Recognizing speech in one language and rendering it in another is translation — the exam's tell for this pair (audio-in, different-language-out).

b.text: The same app also produces same-language French captions for a hearing-impaired attendee in the front row.
b.why: Audio in, same-language text out is plain speech-to-text; no language crosses, so there is nothing to translate.

pairs.dimension: reading literal text vs describing the scene

a.text: Extract the serial number printed on a photographed equipment label.
a.why: OCR/Read extracts the literal text present in the image — 'extract readable text from an image' is the exam stem.

b.text: Generate a one-sentence natural-language description of what the photo shows.
b.why: Captioning (VisualFeatures.CAPTION) describes the scene — it does not read text within it.

pairs.dimension: reading pixels into text vs turning a text prompt into pixels

a.text: A scanning app reads the printed address block off a photographed envelope into structured text fields.
a.why: OCR converts existing pixels into text — the input is an image, the output is text.

b.text: A design tool takes the prompt 'a flat icon of a blue rocket' and produces a brand-new PNG that never existed before.
b.why: Image generation (client.images.generate with gpt-image-1 / DALL·E) runs the opposite direction — text prompt in, synthesized pixels out — the exam's direction-flip trap on this pair.

pairs.dimension: one label for the whole image vs a located box per object

a.text: Decide whether each uploaded photo is 'defective part' or 'good part'.
a.why: Classification assigns one label to the entire image.

b.text: Mark where every part sits on the conveyor image with bounding boxes.
b.why: Bounding boxes per object is the exam's tell for detection — the classic vision confusion.

pairs.dimension: a list of terms vs new condensed sentences

a.text: Return ['pricing', 'battery life', 'customer support'] from a batch of reviews.
a.why: Key phrases return a list of important terms — no new prose is written.

b.text: Condense the same reviews into three fresh sentences capturing the overall feedback.
b.why: Summarization writes new condensed sentences — the output-shape contrast the corpus tests (pair #14).

pairs.dimension: a dedicated privacy filter vs general-purpose entity extraction

a.text: A lightweight app must find and redact every email address and phone number in customer messages before storing them.
a.why: PII detection is the dedicated capability that identifies and can redact sensitive personal data such as phone numbers and email addresses (the exam calls it 'the most direct privacy-focused capability').

b.text: The same app also tags every person, organization, and location mentioned in the messages for a searchable index.
b.why: Entity recognition is broader extraction across categories — people, places, organizations — not the dedicated redaction-focused feature PII detection is.

pairs.dimension: labeling who spoke vs producing spoken audio

a.text: A meeting transcript must attribute each section of the recorded audio to the correct participant.
a.why: Diarization identifies and separates speakers within incoming audio, labeling who spoke each portion of the transcript (the exam calls it 'audio speaker attribution').

b.text: Once the transcript is finalized, a narrator voice reads the meeting summary aloud for a podcast feed.
b.why: Synthesis converts text into human-like voice output — the opposite pipeline stage from diarizing existing audio.

pairs.dimension: converting speech within/into audio vs converting written text between languages

a.text: A developer needs live audio captioning of a video conference in real time, same language, for hearing-impaired participants.
a.why: Azure AI Speech provides the real-time speech-to-text pipeline for live audio — the standard service for captioning, distinct from cross-language text conversion.

b.text: A retailer needs to convert written product descriptions from English into 20 other languages as text.
b.why: Azure AI Translator provides neural machine translation between languages for text — the exam's contrast is audio-pipeline service vs cross-language text service, not a workload overlap (pair #29).
